newsitem.title: UK: UK's Queen holds golden wedding party for 8,000.
newsitem.headline: UK's Queen holds golden wedding party for 8,000.

text.p: Britain's Queen Elizabeth threw open her garden gates on Tuesday to welcome in 4,000 couples who share with her the increasingly rare achievement of a marriage that has lasted for 50 years.
The queen and her husband Prince Philip invited couples from all around the world who married, as they did, in 1947 to a special Golden Wedding garden party at Buckingham Palace.
It is one of numerous events planned for this year to mark the royal wedding anniversary in November.
Couples who responded to newspaper advertisements inviting them to apply for invitations have flown to Britain from all around the world for the occasion.

Nearly 600 couples from Australia applied but only 50 were granted invitations in the palace's random selection. They went to the Australian embassy in London on Tuesday to collect the coveted invitations.

"They were so excited they got here 40 minutes early," said Jane Byford, a spokeswoman at Australia House, as she lined the couples up to have commemorative photographs taken. "They're going to have a wonderful time at the palace."
The garden party was due to begin at 1630 BST (1530 GMT) but the gates to the palace garden in central London were open to the guests shortly after 1500 BST.
"It's something you wouldn't even dream about," said Dutch-born Ricky Kroon, who says her husband fell in love with her over half a century ago when he saw her coming out of a stable cuddling a lamb.
"It's too easy to get a divorce these days," said Kroon, "Young people don't realise you have to work at a marriage to make it work."
Only about ten percent of the guests will get to meet the queen and only a very privileged few will get to join her for tea in the royal tent.
But all the men are expected to wear top hat and tails and the women hats and gloves.

Royal garden parties have been held since the 1860s. The three that take place in London every summer are normally attended by about 8,000 people, many from government, the civil service and the armed forces.
For Britons, the golden wedding celebrations are a reminder of a now distant era when the royals were the nation's first family, setting a moral benchmark for their subjects to follow.
The image was shattered by the bitter and highly public breakdown of heir-to-the-throne Prince Charles' marriage to Princess Diana and the confessions of both that they had affairs.
All three of the queen's four children who married are now divorced. Her youngest son Prince Edward is still single while her daughter Princess Anne has remarried.
The younger royals have even managed to steal the thunder from Elizabeth and Philip this week.
Princess Diana has raised criticism by being photographed holidaying with the controversial boss of Harrods store.
At the same time, her ex-husband Prince Charles is reported to be planning a big 50th birthday party for his lover, Camilla Parker Bowles, whom Diana blamed for the breakdown of their marriage.
